claims.claim: The neural representation of gravity is thought to solve the ambiguity between gravity and inertial accelerations by multisensory statistical inference.
claims.source: The neural representation of gravity is thought to solve this ambiguity by multisensory statistical inference (Angelaki et al., 1999; Merfeld et al., 1999; Angelaki et al., 2004; Laurens et al., 2013b).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior research on multisensory integration for gravity perception.

claims.claim: An internal model of gravity has been shown to benefit the anticipation of a free falling object motion.
claims.source: An internal model of gravity has been shown to benefit the anticipation of a free falling object motion (Zago and Lacquaniti, 2005; Zago et al., 2008; Lacquaniti et al., 2013), as well as the visual perception of allocentric vertical (Van Pelt et al., 2005; De Vrijer et al., 2008; Elmore et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior experimental work.

claims.claim: An internal model of gravity has been shown to benefit the visual perception of allocentric vertical.
claims.source: An internal model of gravity has been shown to benefit the anticipation of a free falling object motion (Zago and Lacquaniti, 2005; Zago et al., 2008; Lacquaniti et al., 2013), as well as the visual perception of allocentric vertical (Van Pelt et al., 2005; De Vrijer et al., 2008; Elmore et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior experimental work.

claims.claim: The compensation hypothesis assumes the internal model of gravity is used to predict and compensate for its mechanical effects on the body.
claims.source: One influential viewpoint assumes a need for compensation; i.e., the internal model of gravity is used to predict and compensate for its mechanical effects on the body.
claims.evidence: This is a description of one hypothesis being tested, supported by citations to prior work on force field adaptation.

claims.claim: The compensation hypothesis has been motivated by experimental findings on arm movements in the presence of externally applied Coriolis, viscous force fields and interaction torques.
claims.source: This hypothesis has been motivated by experimental findings on arm movements in the presence of externally applied Coriolis, viscous force fields and interaction torques (Shadmehr and Mussa-Ivaldi, 1994; Gribble and Ostry, 1999; Pigeon et al., 2003).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior experimental work.

claims.claim: The main benefit of a compensation strategy would be the simplification of motor planning by allowing for invariant trajectories.
claims.source: The main benefit of a compensation strategy would be the simplification of motor planning by allowing for invariant trajectories (Hollerbach and Flash, 1982; Atkeson and Hollerbach, 1985).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior theoretical work.

claims.claim: The effort optimization hypothesis proposes that the internal model of gravity could be used to predict and take advantage of its mechanical effects on the body.
claims.source: An alternative perspective is based on a need for effort optimization, i.e., the internal model of gravity could be used to predict and take advantage of its mechanical effects on the body.
claims.evidence: This is a description of the alternative hypothesis being tested.

claims.claim: Adaptation to the Earth's gravity field has allowed control policies to evolve that take advantage of environmental dynamics.
claims.source: It has been proposed that adaptation to the Earth's gravity field has allowed control policies to evolve that take advantage of environmental dynamics – use gravity as an assistive force to accelerate downward movements and as a resistive force to decelerate upward movements.
claims.evidence: This is a theoretical proposal that is being tested in the manuscript.

claims.claim: The effort optimization strategy has been formalized into a Minimum Smooth-Effort model.
claims.source: This strategy, which has been formalized into a Minimum Smooth-Effort model, would result in movement kinematics that varies with direction (Berret et al., 2008a; Gaveau et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work developing the model.

claims.claim: Upward movements were shown to have shorter time to peak velocity and larger curvature than downward movements.
claims.source: Indeed, upward movements were shown to have shorter time to peak velocity and larger curvature than downward movements, but such comparisons were until now largely qualitative (Papaxanthis et al., 1998b; Gentili et al., 2007).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior experimental work.

claims.claim: The firing properties of extensor motoneurons obey different rules from those of flexor motoneurons.
claims.source: For example, the firing properties of extensor motoneurons (pulling the arm downwards when upright) are known to obey different rules from those of flexor motoneurons (pulling upwards when uptight; Cotel et al., 2009; Wilson et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research on motoneuron properties.

claims.claim: Muscle force production generated by eccentric contraction obeys differing rules from concentric contraction.
claims.source: In addition, muscle force production generated by eccentric contraction (elongation, e.g. downward movements for flexors) is also known to obey differing rules from concentric contraction (e.g. upward movement for flexors; for a review see Enoka, 1996).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a review article.

claims.claim: If directional asymmetries originate from asymmetric firing of flexor/extensor motoneurons, they should persist in the absence of gravity because motoneurons properties are not expected to change during the short zero-G phase of a parabolic flight.
claims.source: If directional asymmetries originate from asymmetric firing of flexor/extensor motoneurons, they should persist in the absence of gravity because motoneurons properties are not expected to change during the short zero-G phase of a parabolic flight (Ishihara et al., 1996, 2002; for a review see Nagatomo et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: This is a prediction based on prior knowledge about motoneuron properties, supported by citations.

claims.claim: If directional asymmetries originate from eccentric versus concentric force production differences, directional asymmetries should cease to exist instantly in 0g because movement dynamics no longer differ for upward and downward movements.
claims.source: On the other hand, if they originate from eccentric versus concentric force production differences, directional asymmetries should cease to exist instantly in 0g because movement dynamics no longer differ for upward and downward movements (Enoka, 1996).
claims.evidence: This is a prediction based on prior knowledge about muscle force production, supported by a citation.

claims.claim: If directional asymmetries originate from neural planning processes that take advantage of the internal model of gravity, following a gradual recalibration of the gravity internal model, directional asymmetries should progressively decrease towards new optimal zero-G values.
claims.source: Alternatively, however, if directional asymmetries originate from neural planning processes that take advantage of the internal model of gravity, following a gradual recalibration of the gravity internal model, directional asymmetries should progressively decrease towards new optimal zero-G values (McIntyre et al., 2001; Izawa et al., 2008; Snaterse et al., 2011).
claims.evidence: This is a prediction based on prior work on sensorimotor adaptation, supported by citations.

claims.claim: Directional asymmetries are gradually eliminated during repeated exposure to the zero-G phase of parabolic flight.
claims.source: In support of the effort optimization hypothesis, we show that directional asymmetries are gradually eliminated during repeated exposure to the zero-G phase of parabolic flight.
claims.evidence: This is a main finding of the study, supported by experimental data from Experiment 2.

claims.claim: Fifteen humans performed arm movements around the shoulder joint in different directions.
claims.source: We asked fifteen humans to perform arm movements around the shoulder joint in different directions (Figure 1A), whereby the work of gravity torque is systematically varied (Figure 1B), while other dynamic variables (interaction torques, Coriolis and centripetal forces) are constant (see Figure 1—figure supplement 1 for a geometrical illustration of the mechanical system and details on gravity torque computations).
claims.evidence: This describes the experimental design of Experiment 1.

claims.claim: The work of gravity torque is systematically varied across different movement directions.
claims.source: We asked fifteen humans to perform arm movements around the shoulder joint in different directions (Figure 1A), whereby the work of gravity torque is systematically varied (Figure 1B), while other dynamic variables (interaction torques, Coriolis and centripetal forces) are constant (see Figure 1—figure supplement 1 for a geometrical illustration of the mechanical system and details on gravity torque computations).
claims.evidence: This is supported by the experimental design and illustrated in Figure 1B.

claims.claim: Other dynamic variables (interaction torques, Coriolis and centripetal forces) are constant across movement directions.
claims.source: We asked fifteen humans to perform arm movements around the shoulder joint in different directions (Figure 1A), whereby the work of gravity torque is systematically varied (Figure 1B), while other dynamic variables (interaction torques, Coriolis and centripetal forces) are constant (see Figure 1—figure supplement 1 for a geometrical illustration of the mechanical system and details on gravity torque computations).
claims.evidence: This is a feature of the experimental design using single-degree of freedom movements.

claims.claim: Symmetry ratio (SR) corresponds to the relative timing of peak velocity.
claims.source: As a measure of the shape of the velocity profile, we define a symmetry ratio (SR: acceleration time divided by the total movement time). SR corresponds to the relative timing of peak velocity (as in Figure 1C) and thus allows quantifying whether arm kinematics remains invariant (compensation hypothesis prediction) or changes (effort optimization hypothesis prediction) with movement direction.
claims.evidence: This is a definition of the kinematic measure used in the study.

claims.claim: The compensation hypothesis predicts that movement kinematics remains unchanged for various gravity torque conditions.
claims.source: Accordingly, the compensation hypothesis predicts that movement kinematics remains unchanged for various gravity torque conditions (Jerk prediction in Figure 1E), whilst the effort optimization hypothesis predicts that movement kinematics strongly correlates (average R = 0.99 [min: 0.986, max: 0.994], p<1e-07) with the amount of gravity torque engaged in the motion (Smooth-Effort prediction in Figure 1E).
claims.evidence: This is a prediction from the Minimum Jerk model simulations, illustrated in Figure 1E.

claims.claim: The effort optimization hypothesis predicts that movement kinematics strongly correlates with the amount of gravity torque engaged in the motion.
claims.source: Accordingly, the compensation hypothesis predicts that movement kinematics remains unchanged for various gravity torque conditions (Jerk prediction in Figure 1E), whilst the effort optimization hypothesis predicts that movement kinematics strongly correlates (average R = 0.99 [min: 0.986, max: 0.994], p<1e-07) with the amount of gravity torque engaged in the motion (Smooth-Effort prediction in Figure 1E).
claims.evidence: This is a prediction from the Minimum Smooth-Effort model simulations, illustrated in Figure 1E, with high correlation coefficients.

claims.claim: The SR dependence on movement direction is a unique feature of effort-related optimization.
claims.source: Importantly, the SR dependence on movement direction (i.e., on gravity torque) is a unique feature of effort-related optimization as minimizing other cost functions that take joint torques into account, but are not directly related to effort, such as the Variance (Harris and Wolpert, 1998) or Torque Change (Uno et al., 1989), predict constant SR as a function of arm movement direction (Figure 1F; see also Figure 1—figure supplement 3 for additional simulations testing the effect of including muscle dynamics into the minimization of end-point Variance).
claims.evidence: This is supported by model simulations comparing different cost functions, illustrated in Figure 1F.

claims.claim: Minimization of an effort-related cost is a necessary and sufficient condition to predict directional asymmetries in the vertical plane.
claims.source: In fact, minimization of an effort-related cost is a necessary and sufficient condition to predict directional asymmetries in the vertical plane (Berret et al., 2008a, 2008b).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior theoretical work.

claims.claim: Participants accomplished rapid arm movements with single-peaked velocity profiles.
claims.source: Participants accomplished rapid arm movements with single-peaked velocity profiles.
claims.evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data in Experiment 1.

claims.claim: Average movement duration did not vary with movement direction (0.40s ± 0.01, SD; F16,224=0.67, p=0.82).
claims.source: Average duration did not vary with movement direction (0.40s ± 0.01, SD; F16,224=0.67, p=0.82).
claims.evidence: This is a statistical result from the experimental data in Experiment 1.

claims.claim: Systematic and variable errors were small and independent of movement direction.
claims.source: Because arm movements were visually guided, systematic and variable errors were small and independent of movement direction (-2.5°< SE < 2°; VE < 2.5°; F16,224=1.13, p=0.32 and F16,224=1.02, p=0.44, respectively).
claims.evidence: This is a statistical result from the experimental data in Experiment 1.

claims.claim: SR shows a sigmoidal modulation as a function of movement direction (F16,224=28.36, p<0.001).
claims.source: As illustrated in Figure 2A, SR shows a sigmoidal modulation as a function of movement direction (F16,224=28.36, p<0.001).
claims.evidence: This is a main finding from Experiment 1, supported by statistical analysis and illustrated in Figure 2A.

claims.claim: When SR was regressed against gravity torque, correlation coefficients were high, averaging R = 0.84 [min: 0.67, max: 0.92], p=2.5e-05.
claims.source: When SR was regressed against gravity torque, correlation coefficients were high, averaging R = 0.84 [min: 0.67, max: 0.92], p=2.5e-05 (Figure 2C).
claims.evidence: This is a main finding from Experiment 1, supported by statistical analysis and illustrated in Figure 2C.

claims.claim: SR was independent of movement duration (average correlation coefficient for duration R = 0.22 [min: 0.04, max: 0.57], p=0.41).
claims.source: Furthermore, SR was independent of movement duration and movement amplitude (average correlation coefficient for duration R = 0.22 [min: 0.04, max: 0.57], p=0.41, see Figure 2—figure supplement 1A; for amplitude R = 0.29 [min: 0.02, max: 0.69], p=0.26, see Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
claims.evidence: This is a statistical result from Experiment 1, illustrated in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claims.claim: SR was independent of movement amplitude (R = 0.29 [min: 0.02, max: 0.69], p=0.26).
claims.source: Furthermore, SR was independent of movement duration and movement amplitude (average correlation coefficient for duration R = 0.22 [min: 0.04, max: 0.57], p=0.41, see Figure 2—figure supplement 1A; for amplitude R = 0.29 [min: 0.02, max: 0.69], p=0.26, see Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
claims.evidence: This is a statistical result from Experiment 1, illustrated in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claims.claim: Arm kinematics is selectively modulated according to the gravity torque requirements of the movement.
claims.source: Thus, arm kinematics is selectively modulated according to the gravity torque requirements of the movement, as predicted by the Smooth-Effort model and quantified by high correlation coefficients between predicted and experimental SR values (average R = 0.82 [min: 0.61, max: 0.91], p=5.6e-05; compare Figure 1D and E to Figure 2A and C, respectively).
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data and model predictions in Experiment 1.

claims.claim: High correlation coefficients exist between predicted and experimental SR values (average R = 0.82 [min: 0.61, max: 0.91], p=5.6e-05).
claims.source: Thus, arm kinematics is selectively modulated according to the gravity torque requirements of the movement, as predicted by the Smooth-Effort model and quantified by high correlation coefficients between predicted and experimental SR values (average R = 0.82 [min: 0.61, max: 0.91], p=5.6e-05; compare Figure 1D and E to Figure 2A and C, respectively).
claims.evidence: This is a statistical result comparing model predictions to experimental data.

claims.claim: Eleven participants performed fast and visually guided single-degree of freedom arm reaching movements in two directions during 5 parabolas in zero-G conditions.
claims.source: Eleven participants performed fast and visually guided single-degree of freedom arm reaching movements in two directions (toward the head and toward the feet, Figure 3A), in zero-G conditions during 5 parabolas (P1-P5) of a flight where centrifugal manoeuvers allow cancellation of gravity effects in the plane's frame of reference.
claims.evidence: This describes the experimental design of Experiment 2.

claims.claim: Arm movements were planar with comparable systematic and variable errors for different gravity and direction conditions.
claims.source: Arm movements were planar with comparable systematic and variable errors for different gravity and direction conditions (shoulder abduction-adduction and internal/external rotation < 3.1°; -3°< SE < 3.3°; VE < 3.4°; gravity effect on SE, p=0.12 and VE, p=0.27; direction effect on SE, p=0.41 and VE, p=0.35).
claims.evidence: This is a statistical result from the experimental data in Experiment 2.

claims.claim: Velocity profiles were single-peaked in both one-G and zero-G conditions.
claims.source: Velocity profiles were single-peaked in both one-G and zero-G conditions and average movement durations ranged between 0.40s and 0.54s (on average, 0.45±0.13s), without any statistical difference between gravity conditions (F5,50=1.274, p=0.29) and movement direction (F1,10=0.549, p=0.48).
claims.evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data in Experiment 2.

claims.claim: Average movement durations ranged between 0.40s and 0.54s without any statistical difference between gravity conditions (F5,50=1.274, p=0.29) and movement direction (F1,10=0.549, p=0.48).
claims.source: Velocity profiles were single-peaked in both one-G and zero-G conditions and average movement durations ranged between 0.40s and 0.54s (on average, 0.45±0.13s), without any statistical difference between gravity conditions (F5,50=1.274, p=0.29) and movement direction (F1,10=0.549, p=0.48).
claims.evidence: This is a statistical result from the experimental data in Experiment 2.

claims.claim: Optimization to the zero-G environment no longer predicts direction-dependent differences in velocity profiles.
claims.source: Figure 3B shows the SR values predicted from the Smooth-Effort model for upward (red) and downward (blue) arm movements, both in one-G and zero-G environments. Optimization to the zero-G environment no longer predicts direction-dependent differences in velocity profiles, as was the case in one-G.
claims.evidence: This is a prediction from the Smooth-Effort model simulations for zero-G, illustrated in Figure 3B.

claims.claim: SR slowly converged towards the new direction-independent optimal value in zero-G (gravity condition and movement direction interaction effect, F5,50=10.54, p<0.001).
claims.source: In line with the effort optimization hypothesis, which predicts gradual adaptation to the zero-G environment, SR slowly converged towards the new direction-independent optimal value in zero-G (Figure 3C; gravity condition and movement direction interaction effect, F5,50=10.54, p<0.001).
claims.evidence: This is a main finding from Experiment 2, supported by statistical analysis and illustrated in Figure 3C.

claims.claim: Directional asymmetries persisted early in zero-G (p=4.8e-05 for P1 and p=1.09e-03 for P2).
claims.source: Importantly, directional asymmetries persisted early in zero-G (p=4.8e-05 for P1 and p=1.09e-03 for P2).
claims.evidence: This is a statistical result from Experiment 2.

claims.claim: During initial exposure to zero-G, the brain still uses the internal model of the one-G environment to plan arm movements.
claims.source: This indicates that, during initial exposure to zero-G, the brain still uses the internal model of the one-G environment to plan arm movements.
claims.evidence: This is an inference drawn from the persistence of directional asymmetries in early zero-G parabolas.

claims.claim: Directional asymmetries progressively disappeared in the following parabolas (post-hoc, p=0.34 for P3, p=0.92 for P4, and p=0.99 for P5).
claims.source: However, directional asymmetries progressively disappeared in the following parabolas, suggesting a gradual re-optimization of motor commands through sensorimotor adaptation to the zero-G environment (post-hoc, p=0.34 for P3, p=0.92 for P4, and p=0.99 for P5).
claims.evidence: This is a statistical result from Experiment 2.

claims.claim: The progressive disappearance of directional asymmetries suggests a gradual re-optimization of motor commands through sensorimotor adaptation to the zero-G environment.
claims.source: However, directional asymmetries progressively disappeared in the following parabolas, suggesting a gradual re-optimization of motor commands through sensorimotor adaptation to the zero-G environment (post-hoc, p=0.34 for P3, p=0.92 for P4, and p=0.99 for P5).
claims.evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data in Experiment 2.

claims.claim: The progressive change in arm kinematic asymmetries can be well explained as a recalibration of the gravity internal model used for optimal motor planning based on the effort optimization model.
claims.source: The progressive decrease in g (internal model of gravity; green dots in Figure 3E) shows that the progressive change in arm kinematic asymmetries can be well explained as a recalibration of the gravity internal model used for optimal motor planning based on the effort optimization (minimization) model (McIntyre et al., 2001; Izawa et al., 2008; Snaterse et al., 2011).
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from fitting the Smooth-Effort model to the experimental data, illustrated in Figure 3E.

claims.claim: The brain develops and uses internal models of the sensor and effector dynamics, as well as physical laws of motion, to optimally interact with the external environment.
claims.source: It is broadly believed that the brain develops and uses internal models of the sensor and effector dynamics, as well as physical laws of motion, to optimally interact with the external environment (Shadmehr and Mussa-Ivaldi, 1994; Conditt et al., 1997; Gribble and Ostry, 1999; Wolpert and Ghahramani, 2000; Pigeon et al., 2003; Todorov, 2004; Ahmed et al., 2008; Scott, 2012).
claims.evidence: This is a statement of established theory in motor control, supported by multiple citations.

claims.claim: Humans use versatile temporal trajectories that are linearly tuned to the gravity torque requirements of the task.
claims.source: First, we have shown that humans use versatile temporal trajectories that are linearly tuned to the gravity torque requirements of the task.
claims.evidence: This is a summary of the main finding from Experiment 1.

claims.claim: Simulations of a Smooth-Effort model can predict not only differences in upward/downward arm movements, but also the linear modulation of endpoint kinematics according to the gravity torque requirements of the movement.
claims.source: Simulations of a Smooth-Effort model, which minimizes a hybrid cost composed of the absolute work of muscular forces (mechanical energy expenditure) and jerk (inverse smoothness of the trajectory) can predict not only differences in upward/downward arm movements, but also the linear modulation of endpoint kinematics according to the gravity torque requirements of the movement.
claims.evidence: This is a summary of the model predictions that match experimental data.

claims.claim: The Smooth-Effort model can be considered an expansion of the minimum Jerk requirement to include how task dynamics shapes movement kinematics.
claims.source: Because the smoothness term of the Smooth-Effort model corresponds to the Jerk, the Smooth-Effort model can be considered an expansion of the minimum Jerk requirement to include how task dynamics shapes movement kinematics.
claims.evidence: This is a theoretical interpretation of the relationship between the Smooth-Effort and Jerk models.

claims.claim: The present results strongly support effort minimization in humans.
claims.source: The present results therefore strongly support effort minimization in humans, further extending the growing idea that perceived effort plays an important role in the tailoring of human motor as well as non-motor behaviors (Bramble and Lieberman, 2004; Walton et al., 2006; Mazzoni et al., 2007; Carrier et al., 2011; Kurzban et al., 2013; Selinger et al., 2015; Farshchiansadegh et al., 2016; Shadmehr et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental results, supported by citations to related work.

claims.claim: The direction-dependent kinematics observed in normal gravity progressively vanishes during repeated exposure to a microgravity environment.
claims.source: Second, we have also shown that the direction-dependent kinematics observed in normal gravity progressively vanishes during repeated exposure to a microgravity environment.
claims.evidence: This is a summary of the main finding from Experiment 2.

claims.claim: Smooth-Effort model simulations nicely predict the adaptation to zero-G.
claims.source: Remarkably, Smooth-Effort model simulations nicely predict this adaptation to zero-G.
claims.evidence: This is a statement about the agreement between model predictions and experimental data.

claims.claim: If the observed direction-dependent kinematics were due to properties of the neuromuscular system, either an abrupt change or no change at all would be expected in the new gravity environment.
claims.source: This is because, if the observed direction-dependent kinematics were due to properties of the neuromuscular system, either an abrupt change or no change at all would be expected in the new gravity environment (Enoka, 1996; Ishihara et al., 1996, 2002; Cotel et al., 2009; Nagatomo et al., 2014; Wilson et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This is a prediction based on prior knowledge about neuromuscular properties, supported by citations.

claims.claim: The fact that neither an abrupt change nor no change happens reveals a central mechanism.
claims.source: The fact that neither happens reveals a central mechanism.
claims.evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental results in Experiment 2.

claims.claim: The observed progressive changes in kinematic asymmetries lead to new optimal values, clearly supporting the hypothesis of a progressive re-optimization procedure originating from planning processes.
claims.source: Furthermore, the fact that the observed progressive changes in kinematic asymmetries lead to new optimal values clearly supports the hypothesis of a progressive re-optimization procedure originating from planning processes (Izawa et al., 2008; Snaterse et al., 2011; Selinger et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental results, supported by citations to related work.

claims.claim: The present findings on arm movements extend and supplement the recent results of Selinger and collaborators on human walking.
claims.source: The present findings on arm movements extend and supplement the recent results of Selinger and collaborators on human walking (Selinger et al., 2015), suggesting that i) the brain can easily and progressively adapt motor patterns to reduce energy expenditure and ii) energy-related criteria (such as effort) are not only the result of, but actually tailor, motor patterns.
claims.evidence: This is a comparison to related work, supported by a citation.

claims.claim: The brain can easily and progressively adapt motor patterns to reduce energy expenditure.
claims.source: The present findings on arm movements extend and supplement the recent results of Selinger and collaborators on human walking (Selinger et al., 2015), suggesting that i) the brain can easily and progressively adapt motor patterns to reduce energy expenditure and ii) energy-related criteria (such as effort) are not only the result of, but actually tailor, motor patterns.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental results and comparison to related work.

claims.claim: Energy-related criteria (such as effort) are not only the result of, but actually tailor, motor patterns.
claims.source: The present findings on arm movements extend and supplement the recent results of Selinger and collaborators on human walking (Selinger et al., 2015), suggesting that i) the brain can easily and progressively adapt motor patterns to reduce energy expenditure and ii) energy-related criteria (such as effort) are not only the result of, but actually tailor, motor patterns.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental results and comparison to related work.

claims.claim: The compensation hypothesis assumes that the brain uses internal models of perturbing forces for their compensation such that stereotypic trajectories can be maintained.
claims.source: The present results and conclusions stand in contrast to a broad view that the brain uses internal models of perturbing forces for their compensation such that stereotypic trajectories can be maintained (Hollerbach and Flash, 1982; Atkeson and Hollerbach, 1985; Shadmehr and Mussa-Ivaldi, 1994).
claims.evidence: This is a description of the compensation hypothesis, supported by citations.

claims.claim: The compensation hypothesis has been challenged by results of studies that quantified velocity profiles and revealed that the temporal organization of arm kinematics shows a small, yet consistent, dependence on movement direction, speed and load.
claims.source: Although very influential, such a compensation hypothesis has been challenged by results of studies that quantified velocity profiles and revealed that the temporal organization of arm kinematics shows a small, yet consistent, dependence on movement direction, speed and load (Papaxanthis et al., 1998b; Gaveau et al., 2011, 2014).
claims.evidence: This is a statement about prior work that challenged the compensation hypothesis, supported by citations.

claims.claim: Virji-Babul et al. (1994) reported regression slopes of SR over movement amplitude that significantly differed between upward and downward movements.
claims.source: For example, Virji-Babul et al. (1994) reported regression slopes of SR over movement amplitude that significantly differed between upward and downward movements (see Figure 2C in Virji-Babul et al., 1994).
claims.evidence: This is a citation to prior work that found results inconsistent with the compensation hypothesis.

claims.claim: The consistent observation of negative periods on the phasic activation of arm muscles suggests that muscular activity does not compensate gravity torque.
claims.source: Also, the consistent observation of negative periods on the phasic activation of arm muscles, resulting from the subtraction of the hypothesized gravity-compensatory activity from the full muscle activation (Flanders et al., 1996), suggest that muscular activity does not compensate gravity torque (Gaveau et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: This is a statement about prior work that found results inconsistent with the compensation hypothesis, supported by citations.

claims.claim: Recent studies have framed motor adaptation as a process of re-optimization.
claims.source: For example, recent studies, which framed motor adaptation as a process of re-optimization (Izawa et al., 2008; Crevecoeur et al., 2009; Gaveau et al., 2011; Cluff and Scott, 2015), have reported subtly altered trajectories – by contrast to the traditional compensation view that assumes invariant trajectories.
claims.evidence: This is a statement about recent theoretical developments in motor control, supported by citations.

claims.claim: Newly constructed/calibrated internal models may serve trajectory optimization rather than external force compensation.
claims.source: Thus, newly constructed/calibrated internal models may serve trajectory optimization rather than external force compensation.
claims.evidence: This is a theoretical interpretation based on recent work on motor adaptation.

claims.claim: The present results demonstrate the propensity of the motor system for multiple control policies whose temporal organization shows small, but systematic, differences, such as to allow minimization of motor effort in our daily living ubiquitous gravity environment.
claims.source: The present results provide further support for this notion and demonstrate the propensity of the motor system for multiple control policies (i.e., trajectories) whose temporal organization shows small, but systematic, differences, such as to allow minimization of motor effort in our daily living ubiquitous gravity environment.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental results.

claims.claim: Directional asymmetries in the vertical plane have been observed in multi-articular arm reaching, reaching to grasp, grasping, hand drawing, and whole-body sit-to-stand / stand-to-sit movements.
claims.source: Specifically, directional asymmetries in the vertical plane (upwards versus downwards) have also been observed in multi-articular arm reaching, reaching to grasp, grasping, hand drawing, and whole-body sit-to-stand / stand-to-sit movements (Papaxanthis et al., 1998c, 2003, 2005; Yamamoto and Kushiro, 2014).
claims.evidence: This is a statement about prior work showing directional asymmetries in various types of movements, supported by citations.

claims.claim: The directional tuning of movement kinematics is a general feature of motor control that may reflect an evolutionary and/or developmental advantage for effort optimization in the Earth's gravity field.
claims.source: Thus, we propose that the directional tuning of movement kinematics is a general feature of motor control that may reflect an evolutionary and/or developmental advantage for effort optimization in the Earth's gravity field (Bramble and Lieberman, 2004; Carrier et al., 2011; Selinger et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This is a proposal based on the experimental results and comparison to related work, supported by citations.

claims.claim: If interaction torques or additional external torques are experienced in the horizontal plane, the Smooth-Effort and Jerk model predictions would be different.

results.result: The brain has evolved an internal model of gravity that is created through multisensory statistical inference to resolve ambiguity between gravity and inertial accelerations, and this model benefits perception and anticipation of object motion.
results.evaluation: Claims C1, C3-C7 collectively establish prior work on internal models of gravity. These claims are well-supported by extensive citations to established literature and represent accepted knowledge in the field. The physics principle (C4) and multisensory integration mechanism (C5) provide theoretical grounding, while C6-C7 cite experimental evidence for functional benefits.

results.result: The compensation hypothesis proposes that the internal model of gravity is used to predict and compensate for gravity's mechanical effects to maintain invariant trajectories, motivated by force field adaptation studies.
results.evaluation: Claims C8-C10 and C62 accurately describe one theoretical framework being tested. These claims are well-supported by citations to relevant prior work on force field adaptation and represent an established viewpoint in motor control, though the current study challenges this hypothesis.

results.result: The effort optimization hypothesis proposes that the internal model of gravity is used to take advantage of gravity's mechanical effects to minimize effort, formalized in the Minimum Smooth-Effort model, with prior qualitative evidence of directional asymmetries.
results.evaluation: Claims C11-C14 describe the alternative hypothesis being tested. C13-C14 are supported by citations to prior work. However, C14 acknowledges that prior comparisons were 'largely qualitative,' which motivates the current quantitative study. The theoretical framework is well-established in cited literature.

results.result: Directional asymmetries could arise from peripheral neuromuscular properties (motoneuron firing or eccentric/concentric contraction differences), leading to distinct predictions for behavior in zero-G: persistence, immediate disappearance, or gradual adaptation, respectively.
results.evaluation: Claims C15-C19 establish alternative explanations and testable predictions. C15-C16 are supported by citations to established neuromuscular physiology. C17-C19 present logical predictions based on this physiology, properly supported by citations. These predictions form the basis for Experiment 2's design.

results.result: Experiment 1 involved 15 participants performing single-degree-of-freedom arm movements in 17 directions with systematically varied gravity torque while other dynamic variables remained constant, with kinematics quantified using symmetry ratio (SR).
results.evaluation: Claims C21-C24 and C79, C84-C88 describe the experimental design and methods for Experiment 1. The design is well-conceived to isolate gravity torque effects (C22-C23). The use of SR as a kinematic measure (C24) is appropriate and standard. Methods for data collection and analysis are clearly described with sufficient detail for replication.

results.result: Model simulations predict that the compensation hypothesis (Minimum Jerk) yields constant SR across directions, while the effort optimization hypothesis (Minimum Smooth-Effort) predicts SR strongly correlates with gravity torque (R=0.99), a unique feature of effort-related optimization.
results.evaluation: Claims C25-C28 present model predictions with quantitative support. The high correlation (R=0.99, p<1e-07) for the Smooth-Effort model (C26) is well-documented. C27 is supported by simulations comparing multiple cost functions (Figure 1F), and C28 is supported by citations to prior theoretical work. The predictions provide clear, testable hypotheses.

results.result: In Experiment 1, participants produced single-peaked velocity profiles with constant duration across directions, and SR showed significant sigmoidal modulation with direction (F16,224=28.36, p<0.001) and high correlation with gravity torque (R=0.84, p=2.5e-05), independent of duration and amplitude.
results.evaluation: Claims C29-C35 report key experimental findings with appropriate statistical tests. The sigmoidal modulation (C32) and correlation with gravity torque (C33) are statistically significant with large effect sizes. Controls showing independence from duration (C34) and amplitude (C35) strengthen the conclusion that SR modulation reflects gravity torque effects specifically. Sample size (n=15, 3060 trials total) appears adequate.

results.result: Arm kinematics is selectively modulated according to gravity torque requirements, with high correlation between Smooth-Effort model predictions and experimental SR values (R=0.82, p=5.6e-05), supporting that humans use versatile temporal trajectories linearly tuned to gravity torque.
results.evaluation: Claims C36-C37 and C50-C51 present the main conclusion from Experiment 1. The high correlation between model and data (R=0.82, p=5.6e-05) provides strong quantitative support. The linear relationship between SR and gravity torque (Figure 2C) matches model predictions (Figure 1E). The conclusion is well-supported by converging evidence from multiple analyses.

results.result: Experiment 2 involved 11 participants performing arm movements in two directions during 5 parabolas of parabolic flight in zero-G, with movements remaining planar and single-peaked with comparable errors and durations across gravity conditions.
results.evaluation: Claims C38-C41 and C80-C83 describe Experiment 2 design and basic kinematic results. The parabolic flight protocol is standard and well-described. Statistical tests show no differences in movement duration (F5,50=1.274, p=0.29) or direction effects (F1,10=0.549, p=0.48), and errors were comparable across conditions, confirming movement quality was maintained.

results.result: SR slowly converged toward direction-independent values in zero-G (interaction F5,50=10.54, p<0.001), with directional asymmetries persisting early (p=4.8e-05 for P1) but progressively disappearing (p=0.99 for P5), suggesting gradual re-optimization through sensorimotor adaptation.
results.evaluation: Claims C42-C47 present the main findings from Experiment 2. The significant interaction effect (C43) and post-hoc tests (C44, C46) provide strong statistical support for gradual adaptation. The pattern of results—persistence followed by gradual disappearance—is inconsistent with peripheral mechanisms and supports central re-optimization. Sample size (n=11) is modest but adequate given the within-subjects design and clear effects.

results.result: The progressive change in kinematic asymmetries during zero-G exposure can be explained as recalibration of the internal gravity model for optimal motor planning, with Smooth-Effort model simulations accurately predicting the adaptation pattern.
results.evaluation: Claims C48, C54-C55 present the interpretation of Experiment 2 results. The model fitting approach (varying internal g parameter) provides quantitative support for the recalibration hypothesis (Figure 3E). The agreement between model predictions and observed gradual adaptation is strong. This interpretation is supported by citations to prior work on sensorimotor adaptation (C48).

results.result: The gradual elimination of directional asymmetries in zero-G, rather than abrupt change or persistence, reveals a central neural mechanism involving progressive re-optimization of motor planning, ruling out peripheral neuromuscular explanations.
results.evaluation: Claims C20, C56-C58 present the key inference from Experiment 2 that distinguishes between hypotheses. The logic is sound: peripheral mechanisms would predict either no change (motoneuron properties) or immediate change (muscle force properties), but gradual adaptation implicates central planning. The experimental results clearly support gradual adaptation, and the inference is well-supported by citations to relevant physiology.

results.result: The brain uses the internal model of gravity to implement control policies that take advantage of gravity to minimize movement effort, with results strongly supporting effort minimization and demonstrating that the motor system uses multiple control policies with systematic temporal differences to minimize effort.
results.evaluation: Claims C2, C53, C60-C61, C68 present the overarching conclusions. These are well-supported by converging evidence from both experiments: quantitative match between effort-optimization model and data (Exp 1), gradual adaptation in zero-G (Exp 2), and ruling out alternative explanations. The conclusions are appropriately supported by citations to related work on effort minimization in other contexts.

results.result: The Smooth-Effort model minimizes a hybrid cost of effort (absolute work of muscle torque) and smoothness (jerk), representing an expansion of the minimum Jerk model to include how task dynamics shapes kinematics.
results.evaluation: Claims C52, C89-C91, C95-C96 describe the theoretical framework of the Smooth-Effort model. The model formulation is clearly described with appropriate citations (C91). The relationship to the minimum Jerk model (C52, C95-C96) is accurately characterized. The necessity of including both effort and smoothness terms is supported by prior work (C91).

results.result: The optimal control problem was solved using a Gauss pseudospectral method, with validation showing that linearized constant gravity torque yields similar results, indicating asymmetries arise from non-zero gravity torque presence rather than variations along movement amplitude.
results.evaluation: Claims C92-C94 describe computational methods and validation. The numerical method (C92) is appropriate and well-cited. The linearized analysis (C93-C94) provides important validation that the key results are robust to modeling assumptions. This strengthens confidence in the model predictions.

results.result: The compensation hypothesis has been challenged by prior studies showing direction-dependent kinematics and muscle activity patterns inconsistent with gravity compensation, with recent work framing adaptation as re-optimization rather than compensation.
results.evaluation: Claims C63-C67 review prior work challenging the compensation hypothesis. The citations appear appropriate and the characterization of prior findings (C64-C65) is specific. The discussion of recent theoretical developments (C66-C67) provides context for the current study's framework. These claims accurately represent the state of the field.

results.result: Directional asymmetries have been observed across multiple movement types, suggesting directional tuning is a general motor control feature that may reflect evolutionary/developmental advantage for effort optimization in Earth's gravity.
results.evaluation: Claims C59, C69-C70 discuss generalizability. C69 is well-supported by citations to prior work on various movement types. C70 is appropriately framed as a proposal ('may reflect') rather than a definitive claim, and is supported by relevant citations. The generalization is reasonable given the breadth of prior findings, though C70 remains somewhat speculative.

results.result: The Smooth-Effort and Jerk models would make different predictions for horizontal plane movements with interaction or external torques, suggesting effort optimization may represent a general motor control principle beyond vertical movements.
results.evaluation: Claims C71-C72 present predictions for future work. While the logic is sound (effort-dependent costs should respond to any torque requirements), these remain untested predictions. C72 is appropriately framed as a proposal for future experiments. The claims are speculative but well-reasoned extensions of the current findings.

results.result: Twenty-six right-handed adults participated across two experiments with appropriate informed consent and ethical approval from regional committees, following Declaration of Helsinki standards.
results.evaluation: Claims C73-C78 describe participant characteristics and ethical procedures. Sample sizes (15 and 11 for Experiments 1 and 2) are reasonable for within-subjects designs. Handedness assessment using Edinburgh test (C75) is standard. Ethical procedures (C74, C76-C78) are appropriately documented. All procedures appear to meet ethical standards.

results.result: The Minimum Torque Change model predicts symmetrical velocity profiles for horizontal single-degree-of-freedom movements under various dynamics, consistent with the current study's simulations.
results.evaluation: Claim C97 accurately cites prior work (Tanaka et al., 2004) on the Minimum Torque Change model and relates it to the current findings (Figure 1F). This supports the conclusion that direction-dependent kinematics are specific to effort-related optimization.
